## Guide: React components for AI chat interfaces

A good AI chat interface needs more than a message list: a composer with attachments and model choice, an answer that streams with sources, a visible thinking state, readable tool calls, and actions under every reply. affectUI has a React component for each of these – one file each, no dependencies, installable with the shadcn CLI.

### The parts of an AI chat UI

Most chat UIs start as a text field and a list of bubbles. What makes an AI product feel finished are the states in between: the moment the model is thinking, the moment it calls a tool, the moment a long answer streams in, and what people can do with an answer afterwards.

- Composer – multi-line input, attachments, model picker, a clear send and stop button
- Streaming answer – text that arrives in pieces without jumping, with sources people can check
- Thinking state – a calm sign that the model is working, ideally with what it is doing
- Tool calls – which tool ran, with what input, how long it took and what came back
- Message actions – copy, regenerate, feedback and read aloud under each reply
- Empty state – prompt ideas, so the first message isn't a blank page

### Composer

The composer is where people spend the most time. It should grow with the text, keep the send button reachable, and let people switch models or modes without leaving the field. Enter sends, Shift+Enter adds a line. affectUI's Chat Composer brings a model picker, voice input and app connections; the Model Picker shows speed, quality and cost per model, and the Prompt Library keeps reusable prompts with variables.

affectUI: [Chat Composer](https://www.affectui.com/components/chat-composer), [Model Picker](https://www.affectui.com/components/model-picker), [Prompt Library](https://www.affectui.com/components/prompt-library)

### Answers with sources

Long answers should stream into a layout that doesn't shift, so people can start reading before the end arrives. When the model used sources – documents, web pages, tools – show them as small cards next to the answer and link each claim to its source with a numbered citation.

affectUI: [AI Answer](https://www.affectui.com/components/ai-answer), [Cited Answer](https://www.affectui.com/components/cited-answer)

### Thinking and progress

A spinner says nothing. A thinking state can say what the model is doing – searching, reading, comparing – and how long it has been at it. For short waits a small loader is enough; for longer reasoning, a panel with the steps keeps people from wondering whether anything is happening.

affectUI: [Thinking State](https://www.affectui.com/components/thinking-state), [Thinking Loader](https://www.affectui.com/components/thinking-loader), [Context Window](https://www.affectui.com/components/context-window)

### Tool calls

When an agent calls tools, show each call in one line – name, status, time – and let people open it to see the arguments and the result. Failed calls need a visible error and a retry, not a silent gap in the conversation.

affectUI: [Tool Call Card](https://www.affectui.com/components/tool-call-card)

### Actions under every reply

Copy, regenerate, thumbs up or down and read aloud belong under each answer – quiet until people need them. Regenerating should keep the earlier versions so people can switch back.

affectUI: [Message Actions](https://www.affectui.com/components/message-actions)

### Install

Every component is a single .tsx file with its styles inside – no Tailwind, no animation library. Add it with the shadcn CLI and import it from components/ui. The components are UI only and take plain props, so you can connect any backend – the Vercel AI SDK, LangChain or your own API.

```
npx shadcn@latest add https://www.affectui.com/r/message-actions.json
```

### Questions

**Do these components need Tailwind CSS?** No. Each affectUI component carries its own styles and only needs React 19. It works in projects with or without Tailwind.

**Can I use them with the Vercel AI SDK?** Yes. The components only render UI and take props such as the message text, status and sources, so you pass in whatever your AI SDK, LangChain chain or own API returns.

**Are they accessible?** Status changes such as thinking or writing are announced to screen readers, every action is a real button with a label, focus is visible, and motion respects the reduced-motion setting.

**Which ones are free?** Message Actions, Thinking Loader and Tool Call Card are among the free, MIT-licensed components. Chat Composer, AI Answer and Thinking State are part of affectUI Pro.

---

## Guide: How to build an agent dashboard in React

An agent dashboard has to answer five questions at a glance: what is running, who started whom, what needs a person, how long and how much it took, and what went wrong. Build it from a few focused views – an inbox of runs, a tree of agents, a timeline, a trace and approvals – rather than one big table.

### Start from the questions

A dashboard for agents is a control room. People open it to check on work they handed off, so each view should answer one question fast.

- What's running, waiting or done? – an inbox grouped by state
- Who started whom? – a tree from the orchestrator down to its sub-agents
- Where is every agent right now? – lanes on a timeline
- Where did the time and money go? – a trace waterfall per run
- What needs me? – approvals and questions, right where the work is

### An inbox of runs

Background agents need a place where their work lands. A list or board grouped by needs you, running and done – with live clocks and status – lets people triage dozens of runs without opening each one.

affectUI: [Agent Inbox](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-inbox), [Decision Inbox](https://www.affectui.com/components/decision-inbox), [Delegate Board](https://www.affectui.com/components/delegate-board)

### Multi-agent runs: tree and lanes

When an orchestrator hands work to sub-agents, a tree shows who started whom, with status, cost and time on every card and costs adding up per branch. Lanes show the same run over time: one lane per agent, tasks growing into now, and hand-offs drawn between them.

affectUI: [Agent Tree](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-tree), [Agent Lanes](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-lanes), [Agent Graph](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-graph)

### Traces: time and cost per step

For one run, a trace waterfall answers where the time and money went: every LLM call, tool call and sub-agent as a bar on a shared timeline, with duration and cost next to it. Comparing the plan with what actually happened shows which step made a run late.

affectUI: [Trace Waterfall](https://www.affectui.com/components/trace-waterfall), [Plan vs Actual](https://www.affectui.com/components/plan-vs-actual), [Agent Plan](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-plan)

### People in the loop

Agents that can send emails, spend money or change data need a way to ask first. Put the question where the work is – on the task, in the run – with the exact action, its inputs and two clear answers.

affectUI: [Approval Card](https://www.affectui.com/components/approval-card), [Permission Request](https://www.affectui.com/components/permission-request), [Agent Steering](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-steering)

### Cost and limits

Show spend against a budget and token use against the context window, so people see a problem before a run fails.

affectUI: [Usage Meter](https://www.affectui.com/components/usage-meter), [Context Window](https://www.affectui.com/components/context-window)

### Putting it together

Start with an app shell – sidebar, page, and a work area on the right for details – and put the inbox on the home view. Open a run into its tree or trace, and keep approvals visible in the sidebar or as a badge. All views take plain data as props and animate their own changes, so they update in place as your agents report progress.

affectUI: [Agent Run](https://www.affectui.com/screens/agent-run), [App Shell Workspace Inset](https://www.affectui.com/screens/app-shell-workspace)

### Questions

**Do I need WebSockets for a live agent dashboard?** Any way of getting updates works – WebSockets, server-sent events or polling. The components only need the latest data as props; they animate the change themselves.

**Which framework does this work with?** Any React 19 setup – Next.js, Vite, Remix or React Router. The components don't depend on a framework or a state library.

**Can I show runs from LangGraph, CrewAI or the OpenAI Agents SDK?** Yes. Map your framework's runs, steps and tool calls to the components' props – an id, a name, a status, times and costs are usually all they need.

---

## Guide: Human-in-the-loop UI: approvals, permissions and autonomy

Human-in-the-loop UI lets agents act on their own where it's safe and ask where it isn't. The core patterns are an approval card for single actions, a permission request for access, an autonomy setting that decides when to ask, steering for running work, and a review step for changes.

### Ask about the action, not in general

"The agent wants to continue" is not something people can judge. A good approval shows exactly what will happen – send this email to these people, charge this amount, delete these files – with the inputs visible and two clear answers. Keep it next to the work it belongs to.

affectUI: [Approval Card](https://www.affectui.com/components/approval-card), [Decision Inbox](https://www.affectui.com/components/decision-inbox)

### Permissions: scoped and reversible

When an agent needs access to a tool or data, ask once with a clear scope – read or write, this folder or all, this time or always – and make it easy to take back later.

affectUI: [Permission Request](https://www.affectui.com/components/permission-request), [Integration Settings](https://www.affectui.com/components/integration-settings)

### Autonomy: decide when the agent asks

Not every action needs a person. Let people choose per kind of action: always ask, ask only when risky, or run on its own. Destructive actions like deleting or spending money should stay locked to ask first.

affectUI: [Autonomy Dial](https://www.affectui.com/components/autonomy-dial)

### Steering work that is already running

People notice problems while an agent works. Let them queue a note the agent picks up at its next step, or interrupt it, instead of stopping the whole run and starting over.

affectUI: [Agent Steering](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-steering), [Agent Plan](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-plan)

### Reviewing what changed

Before changes go live, show them as a diff and let people accept or reject parts instead of all or nothing. When agents queue many actions, a review workspace sorted by risk lets people go through them one at a time.

affectUI: [Inline Diff](https://www.affectui.com/components/inline-diff), [Review Center](https://www.affectui.com/components/review-center)

### Questions

**When should an AI agent ask for approval?** Before actions that are hard to undo or affect other people: sending messages, spending money, deleting data, publishing, or changing permissions. Reading and drafting usually don't need approval.

**How do I avoid approval fatigue?** Ask about concrete actions, group similar ones, and let people raise the agent's autonomy for actions they trust – so they only see the decisions that matter.

---

## Guide: How to show tool calls in an AI agent UI

Show every tool call as one line – tool, short summary, status and time – and let people open it for the exact arguments and result. Group many calls into a summary, show failures with a retry instead of hiding them, and move to a trace or graph view once a run makes dozens of calls across several agents.

### One line per call

Raw JSON in the chat is unreadable and a bare spinner hides what the agent is doing. The middle ground is one line per call: the tool's name or logo, a short human summary ("Searched Linear for open bugs"), a status and how long it took. While it runs, the time ticks; when it's done, the line settles.

affectUI: [Tool Call Card](https://www.affectui.com/components/tool-call-card)

### Details on demand

Developers and careful users want the arguments and the result. Keep them one click away, formatted and copyable, so the conversation stays readable for everyone else.

- Arguments as formatted, highlighted JSON – not a single long string
- The result trimmed to what matters, with a way to see all of it
- Copy buttons for both, for debugging and bug reports

### Errors are part of the story

A failed call that disappears leaves people guessing why the answer is wrong. Show the failure in place – what failed and why – with a retry, and let the agent's next attempt appear right after it.

affectUI: [Tool Call Card](https://www.affectui.com/components/tool-call-card), [Fallback Chain](https://www.affectui.com/components/fallback-chain)

### Many calls: group them

Agents often make five or ten calls for one answer. Fold them into a group ("Used 6 tools · 4.2s") that opens on click, so the reply isn't buried under its own work.

affectUI: [Thinking State](https://www.affectui.com/components/thinking-state), [Tool Call Card](https://www.affectui.com/components/tool-call-card)

### Whole runs: trace or graph

Once a run spans several agents and dozens of calls, a list stops working. A trace waterfall shows every call on a timeline with its duration and cost; a graph shows which agents call which tools and how often.

affectUI: [Trace Waterfall](https://www.affectui.com/components/trace-waterfall), [Agent Graph](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-graph), [Agent Run](https://www.affectui.com/screens/agent-run)

### Install

Tool Call Card is free and open source (MIT) – one file, no dependencies.

```
npx shadcn@latest add https://www.affectui.com/r/tool-call-card.json
```

### Questions

**Should I show tool calls to end users at all?** Yes, in a quiet form. One line per call builds trust and explains slow answers; the full arguments and results can stay folded for those who want them.

**How do I show tool calls from the OpenAI or Anthropic APIs?** Map each tool call to a name, its arguments, a status (running, done, failed), start and end times and the result. Those are the props the component needs, whatever API produced them.

---

## Guide: Streaming AI responses in React without layout shift

To stream AI responses without layout shift, render the answer into a container that only grows downward, keep everything around it at a fixed size, show a small thinking state until the first tokens arrive, and add sources and actions in space that's already reserved. Let people scroll freely instead of forcing the view to the bottom.

### Why streamed answers jump



- Elements above the answer change size – a status line that swaps text, a loader that disappears
- Sources, buttons or follow-ups pop in after the text and push it around
- Markdown re-renders: a list or code block changes shape when its closing token arrives
- Auto-scroll fights the reader when they scroll up to read

### Before the first token

The first second matters most. Show a small thinking state right where the answer will appear – ideally with what the model is doing – and let the text take its place without moving anything else.

affectUI: [Thinking Loader](https://www.affectui.com/components/thinking-loader), [Thinking State](https://www.affectui.com/components/thinking-state), [Shimmer Loader](https://www.affectui.com/motion/shimmer-loader)

### While it streams

Append text to one container that grows downward. Keep the status line a fixed height and swap its text in place. If you animate new words, keep it subtle and turn it off for people who ask for reduced motion.

affectUI: [AI Answer](https://www.affectui.com/components/ai-answer), [Text Reveal](https://www.affectui.com/motion/text-reveal)

### Sources, citations and actions

Reserve the space for source cards and the action bar from the start, or add them below the text where they can't push it. Citations work best as small numbered chips inside the sentence that preview their source on hover.

affectUI: [Cited Answer](https://www.affectui.com/components/cited-answer), [Message Actions](https://www.affectui.com/components/message-actions)

### Scrolling

Follow the stream only while the reader is at the bottom. As soon as they scroll up, stop following and show a small "jump to latest" button instead of pulling them back down.

### Swapping content

When a regenerated answer replaces the old one, or a short answer expands, let the box glide to its new height instead of snapping.

affectUI: [Blur Crossfade](https://www.affectui.com/motion/blur-crossfade)

### Questions

**Should I stream word by word or in chunks?** Render what arrives as it arrives. If tokens come in bursts, a light per-word fade smooths it out without slowing the answer down.

**How do I handle markdown while streaming?** Parse the growing text on every update but keep unfinished blocks – an open code fence or table – in a simple form until they close, so their shape doesn't flip.

**Does reduced motion matter for streaming?** Yes. With reduced motion on, show text without animation; affectUI's answer and text components check the setting themselves.

---

## Guide: Model picker UI: letting users choose an LLM

A good model picker shows a short list with what people actually choose by – speed, quality and cost – instead of model names alone, keeps a sensible default, puts reasoning or effort settings next to the model, and makes fallbacks visible when a model fails. Keep it inside the composer, one click away.

### What people choose by

Most people can't tell models apart by name. Show what changes for them: how fast it answers, how good it is for the task, and what it costs – as simple bars or labels, not benchmark tables.

affectUI: [Model Picker](https://www.affectui.com/components/model-picker)

### Keep it in the composer

The picker belongs next to the send button, so people switch per message without leaving the conversation. Show the current model's name in the button, and remember the last choice.

affectUI: [Chat Composer](https://www.affectui.com/components/chat-composer)

### Reasoning and effort

Extended thinking or effort levels change speed and cost a lot. Put them right under the model they belong to, and only show them for models that support them.

### Fallbacks and comparing

Models fail and rate-limit. If your product falls back to another model, show it – which model answered and why – instead of hiding it. For tasks where quality matters, running the same prompt on several models and comparing the results helps people pick.

affectUI: [Fallback Chain](https://www.affectui.com/components/fallback-chain), [Parallel Attempts](https://www.affectui.com/components/parallel-attempts)

### Limits and context

Models differ in context size. When a conversation gets long, show how full the context is before it runs out, not after.

affectUI: [Context Window](https://www.affectui.com/components/context-window), [Context Map](https://www.affectui.com/components/context-map)

### Questions

**Should I let users pick the model at all?** For power users and developers, yes. For everyone else, choose a good default and offer a simple choice like fast or best – and still show which model answered.

**How many models should the picker show?** Three to six covers most products. Group the rest under "More models" so the main list stays scannable.

---

## Guide: How to show AI agent costs and token usage

Show cost where decisions are made: a running total on every run, cost per step in a trace, cost per agent rolling up a tree, and spend against a budget in settings. For tokens, show how full the context window is and what fills it, so people can act before a limit is hit.

### Cost per run and per step

People want to know two things: what did this run cost, and which step made it expensive. A trace waterfall answers both – each LLM call, tool call and sub-agent with its duration, tokens and cost on one timeline.

affectUI: [Trace Waterfall](https://www.affectui.com/components/trace-waterfall), [Plan vs Actual](https://www.affectui.com/components/plan-vs-actual)

### Cost per agent

In multi-agent runs, put each agent's cost on its card and add the costs up per branch, so it's obvious which sub-agent burned the budget.

affectUI: [Agent Tree](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-tree), [Fan-out Grid](https://www.affectui.com/components/fan-out-grid)

### Budgets and plans

For the account as a whole, show spend or credits against the limit, split by what used them, with a daily trend – and a clear warning before the limit, not an error after it.

affectUI: [Usage Meter](https://www.affectui.com/components/usage-meter), [Compact Breakdown](https://www.affectui.com/components/compact-breakdown)

### Tokens and the context window

Token counts mean little on their own. Show the context as a share of the window – system prompt, tools, files, chat – so people can see what to remove or when to compact the conversation.

affectUI: [Context Window](https://www.affectui.com/components/context-window), [Context Map](https://www.affectui.com/components/context-map)

### Formatting money



- Round sensibly: $0.42 for a run, $1,240 for a month – not $0.4183291
- Show the currency once and line numbers up with tabular figures
- Animate totals as they grow, so a live run feels live

affectUI: [Number Ticker](https://www.affectui.com/motion/number-ticker)

### Questions

**Should end users see what an agent costs?** If they pay per use or have a budget, yes – a running total per run and spend against their limit. If you charge a flat price, show it to admins and keep it out of the main interface.

**Where do the cost numbers come from?** From the token counts your model provider returns with every response, multiplied by its prices. The components only display the numbers you pass in.

---

## Guide: How to show what an AI agent is doing

Show an agent's work at three levels: the step it is on right now, with a clock and a plain-language label; the plan it is following, with done, current and upcoming steps; and the whole run as a tree, timeline or trace once several agents or many calls are involved. Each level answers a different question, so show the smallest one that does.

### Pick the view by the question

"What is the agent doing?" means different things at different moments. While waiting for an answer, people want to know that something is happening and what. During a long task, they want to see progress against a plan. After a run, they want to know why it took so long or cost so much.

- Is it working, and on what? – a thinking state or a one-line current step
- How far along is it? – the plan with the current step highlighted
- What did it call? – one line per tool call, details on demand
- Who is doing what? – a tree or lanes when several agents work together
- Where did the time and money go? – a trace waterfall after the run

### The current step

The smallest useful signal is the step in words – "Reading 12 pages", "Comparing prices" – with a clock that keeps ticking. It tells people the agent hasn't stalled and gives them something to judge. Swap the label in place so nothing around it moves, and settle on a check when the step is done.

affectUI: [Thinking Loader](https://www.affectui.com/components/thinking-loader), [Thinking State](https://www.affectui.com/components/thinking-state)

### The plan

For tasks that take minutes, show the plan before or as the agent starts: a short list of steps where the current one is marked and finished ones check off. Letting people edit the plan before it runs catches wrong turns early; comparing the plan with what actually happened shows which step ran over.

affectUI: [Agent Plan](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-plan), [Plan vs Actual](https://www.affectui.com/components/plan-vs-actual)

### Tool calls

Every call to a search, a database or an API is a step people may want to check. Show each one as a line with the tool, a short summary, its status and time, and keep the exact arguments and result one click away.

affectUI: [Tool Call Card](https://www.affectui.com/components/tool-call-card)

### Several agents: tree and lanes

When an orchestrator hands work to sub-agents, a flat log gets confusing fast. A tree shows who started whom, with status, cost and time on each card. Lanes show the same run over time – one lane per agent, so it's clear who was busy when and where work was handed over.

affectUI: [Agent Tree](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-tree), [Agent Lanes](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-lanes), [Agent Handoff](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-handoff)

### After the run: the trace

A trace waterfall puts every LLM call, tool call and sub-agent on one timeline with duration and cost. It is the view for questions like "why did this take four minutes?" – the long bar is the answer.

affectUI: [Trace Waterfall](https://www.affectui.com/components/trace-waterfall), [Agent Graph](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-graph)

### Keep it calm



- Fixed row heights, so a live list doesn't jump as states change
- Plain-language labels first, raw data folded away
- One moving thing at a time – the current step, not the whole screen
- Status changes announced to screen readers, motion off with reduced motion

### Questions

**Should I show the model's reasoning?** Show what the agent is doing, not every token it thinks. A short label per step, with the full reasoning folded away for those who want it, keeps the interface readable.

**How do I get step and status data from my agent framework?** LangGraph, the OpenAI Agents SDK, CrewAI and the Vercel AI SDK all emit events for steps, tool calls and sub-agents. Map each event to an id, a label, a status and start and end times – that is what these components take as props.

**Which of these components are free?** Tool Call Card and Thinking Loader are free and MIT-licensed. Agent Tree, Agent Lanes, Agent Plan and Trace Waterfall are part of affectUI Pro.

---

## Guide: Approval UI for AI agents: what to show before an agent acts

An approval card should show the exact action the agent wants to take, its inputs and a preview of the result, how risky and how reversible it is, and two clear answers – with keyboard shortcuts. Ask only for actions that are hard to undo, batch similar requests, and keep a record with undo for everything that was approved.

### What the card has to show

People approve quickly when they can see what will happen and slowly or blindly when they can't. Every approval needs the same few things, in this order:

- The action in one sentence – "Send this email to 3 people", "Refund $240 to Acme"
- The inputs that matter – recipients, amount, files, target system
- A preview of the result – the email, the diff, the record as it will look
- Risk and reversibility – can this be undone, and who else is affected
- Two answers – Approve and Deny – plus a way to edit before approving

affectUI: [Approval Card](https://www.affectui.com/components/approval-card), [Email Draft](https://www.affectui.com/components/email-draft)

### Risk decides how loud it is

Not every request deserves the same weight. Reading data or drafting text usually needs no approval at all. Sending, paying, deleting and publishing do. Mark the risk on the card, make destructive actions take a deliberate second step, and never pre-select Approve for them.

affectUI: [Approval Card](https://www.affectui.com/components/approval-card), [Permission Request](https://www.affectui.com/components/permission-request)

### Edit instead of deny

Often the agent is almost right – wrong recipient, wrong tone, one line too many. Letting people fix the draft or the diff in place and then approve saves a full round trip. For changes to text or code, accept and reject parts instead of the whole thing.

affectUI: [Email Draft](https://www.affectui.com/components/email-draft), [Inline Diff](https://www.affectui.com/components/inline-diff)

### Timeouts and waiting agents

An agent waiting for approval is a paused run. Show that it's paused and since when, and decide what happens if nobody answers – remind, fall back to a safe default, or cancel. If a countdown runs, pause it while the person is looking at the card.

affectUI: [Approval Card](https://www.affectui.com/components/approval-card), [Agent Inbox](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-inbox)

### Many requests: batch and sort

Agents that work in the background can queue dozens of requests. Collect them in one place, sorted by risk, with two quick answers each – and let people approve similar ones together. When a decision has real trade-offs, show the options and their consequences instead of a yes or no.

affectUI: [Decision Inbox](https://www.affectui.com/components/decision-inbox), [Review Center](https://www.affectui.com/components/review-center), [Decision Tree](https://www.affectui.com/components/decision-tree)

### After approval: a record with undo

Approval isn't the end. Keep a list of what the agent changed, with before and after and an undo per change, so a wrong approval can be taken back. Once people trust an action, let them raise the agent's autonomy for it so it stops asking.

affectUI: [Agent Ledger](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-ledger), [Autonomy Dial](https://www.affectui.com/components/autonomy-dial)

### Questions

**Which agent actions need approval?** Actions that are hard to undo or affect other people: sending messages, spending money, deleting or overwriting data, publishing, and changing access. Reading, searching and drafting usually don't.

**Where should the approval appear?** Next to the work it belongs to – in the chat, on the task or in the run – and in one inbox for background agents, with a badge so people notice it.

**How do I keep people from clicking Approve without reading?** Ask less often and more concretely. When the card shows the exact action and a preview, and routine actions no longer ask, the remaining requests get real attention.

---

## Guide: Multi-agent UI in React: orchestrators, sub-agents and hand-offs

A multi-agent UI has to show structure, time and flow: a tree for who started whom, lanes for who is busy when, hand-offs for what moved between agents, and a grid or queue when one job fans out to many workers. Put cost and status on every agent, add costs up per branch, and show conflicts between agents before they collide.

### Why one chat isn't enough

With one agent, a conversation and a list of tool calls tell the whole story. With an orchestrator and five sub-agents, the same log interleaves everyone's steps and nobody can follow it. Multi-agent work needs views that separate the agents and show how they relate.

### Structure: who started whom

A tree from the orchestrator down to its sub-agents answers the first question. Each card carries the agent's task, status, time and cost, and costs add up per branch, so an expensive sub-agent stands out. A graph works better when agents call each other and shared tools in all directions.

affectUI: [Agent Tree](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-tree), [Agent Graph](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-graph)

### Time: who is busy when

Lanes put each agent on its own row of a shared timeline. Tasks grow into "now" while they run, idle gaps are visible, and hand-offs are drawn between lanes – the view for spotting the agent everyone is waiting on.

affectUI: [Agent Lanes](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-lanes)

### Hand-offs: what moved along

When work passes from agent to agent, the risky part is what gets lost on the way. Show each hand-off with what went along – the brief, the files, the findings – and what was dropped, so a weak result can be traced to where context went missing.

affectUI: [Agent Handoff](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-handoff)

### Fan-out and parallel attempts

Some jobs split into many small tasks for many workers; a grid where every task is a cell that fills in shows progress at a glance. Other jobs run the same task several ways at once and keep the best result – show the attempts side by side and mark the winner.

affectUI: [Fan-out Grid](https://www.affectui.com/components/fan-out-grid), [Parallel Attempts](https://www.affectui.com/components/parallel-attempts), [Agent Findings](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-findings)

### Queue and assignment

When there's more work than agents, show the queue: what's waiting, which worker picks up what, and how fast it moves. Letting people drag work onto an agent – with a preview of when it'll be done – turns the queue into a planning tool.

affectUI: [Agent Queue](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-queue), [Delegate Board](https://www.affectui.com/components/delegate-board)

### Conflicts

Agents working on the same code or document can overwrite each other. Show who is touching which file and where their changes overlap before they merge, and show agents working in a shared document the way a multiplayer editor shows teammates.

affectUI: [Conflict Radar](https://www.affectui.com/components/conflict-radar), [Agent Cursors](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-cursors)

### Talking to the team

People still talk to the orchestrator, not to every agent. A chat with the orchestrator next to a live view of the agents at work keeps the conversation simple and the work visible.

affectUI: [Agent Chat](https://www.affectui.com/screens/agent-chat)

### Questions

**Do these work with LangGraph, CrewAI or the OpenAI Agents SDK?** Yes. The components take plain data – agents with an id, a parent, a task, a status, times and costs – which you map from your framework's run events.

**How many agents can a tree or lane view show?** A tree stays readable with a few dozen agents if branches fold; lanes work best with up to about ten at once. For hundreds of small tasks, use a fan-out grid instead.

**Should end users see every sub-agent?** Usually not by default. Show the orchestrator's progress and a summary, and let people open the tree or lanes when they want to know more.

---

## Guide: Context window UI: showing what fills an LLM's context

Show the context window as a share of its limit, split by what fills it – system prompt, tools, memory, files and the conversation – so people see at a glance what takes the most space. Warn before it's full, let people remove files or compact the conversation in place, and keep long-term memory as a separate, editable list.

### Why show the context at all

When the context fills up, answers get worse, slower and more expensive, and eventually the model forgets the start of the conversation. People can't fix what they can't see. A small view of what's in the context turns a mysterious drop in quality into something they can act on.

### What fills it

A single token count says little. Split it into the parts people recognise:

- System prompt and instructions – usually fixed
- Tool definitions – grow with every connected app
- Memory – what the assistant remembers about the user
- Files and attachments – often the biggest part
- The conversation – grows with every message

affectUI: [Context Window](https://www.affectui.com/components/context-window), [Context Map](https://www.affectui.com/components/context-map)

### How full is it

Show the total as a share of the window, not as "84,213 tokens". A bar or a field of cells reads instantly; color it as it approaches the limit and warn before the next message would overflow, not after the model has dropped something.

affectUI: [Context Window](https://www.affectui.com/components/context-window)

### Let people make room

The fix should sit right next to the problem. Hovering a part highlights how much it takes; files can be removed in one click; and a compact action summarises the older conversation and shows how much space it freed.

affectUI: [Context Window](https://www.affectui.com/components/context-window), [Context Map](https://www.affectui.com/components/context-map)

### Memory is different

Long-term memory outlives a conversation, so it needs its own place: a list people can read, edit and switch off, grouped by topic and showing where each memory came from. Show how much of the context it takes, but manage it in settings rather than in the chat.

affectUI: [Memory Panel](https://www.affectui.com/components/memory-panel)

### Context and cost

Every token in the context is paid for on every request. Showing the context next to usage and budget makes clear why long conversations with big files cost more – and why compacting helps.

affectUI: [Usage Meter](https://www.affectui.com/components/usage-meter)

### Questions

**Where do I get the token counts?** Most model APIs return input and output token counts with every response, and offer a token-counting endpoint or library for counting parts before sending. Pass the counts per part to the component.

**Should every user see the context window?** Power users and developers benefit most. For everyone else, a small indicator that turns into a warning near the limit is enough, with the detailed view one click away.

**What does compacting do?** It replaces older messages with a short summary, keeping the gist while freeing space. Show what was summarised and how much space it saved, so it doesn't feel like the assistant forgot things.

---

## Comparison: affectUI vs shadcn/ui

shadcn/ui gives you general building blocks – buttons, dialogs, inputs – styled with Tailwind. affectUI gives you finished pieces for AI products – chat composers, agent trees, tool calls, approvals – each as one self-contained file. They don't compete: affectUI installs through the shadcn CLI and sits next to shadcn/ui in the same project.

### What each one is



- shadcn/ui – general UI primitives (button, dialog, select, table…) you copy into your project, styled with Tailwind CSS and built on headless libraries
- affectUI – higher-level components, screens and blocks for AI and agent products, each one .tsx file with its own styles and motion, no Tailwind or other dependencies

### Where they differ



- Scope: shadcn/ui covers the basics of any app; affectUI covers what AI products need on top – streaming answers, thinking states, tool calls, multi-agent views, approvals
- Styling: shadcn/ui uses Tailwind classes; affectUI components carry their own CSS with variables for colors, so they work with or without Tailwind
- Finish: shadcn/ui is intentionally plain so you style it; affectUI ships designed states and motion, in two styles (classic and clean)
- Price: shadcn/ui is free; affectUI has free MIT components and a one-time Pro license for the rest

### Using both together

affectUI is a shadcn registry, so the same CLI installs both. Register affectUI once in components.json to use short names, and its components land in components/ui next to your shadcn/ui ones.

```
// components.json
{
  "registries": {
    "@affectui": "https://www.affectui.com/r/{name}.json"
  }
}

// then
npx shadcn@latest add @affectui/tool-call-card
```

### Which to pick



- Building a general app or design system from scratch – start with shadcn/ui
- Building an AI product and want chat, agent and approval UI that looks finished – add affectUI
- Most AI products use both: shadcn/ui for forms and dialogs, affectUI for the AI-specific parts

affectUI: [Chat Composer](https://www.affectui.com/components/chat-composer), [Agent Tree](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-tree), [Tool Call Card](https://www.affectui.com/components/tool-call-card)

### Questions

**Is affectUI built on shadcn/ui?** No. affectUI components are self-contained and don't import shadcn/ui, but they install through the shadcn CLI and live in the same components/ui folder.

**Does affectUI need Tailwind?** No. Each component carries its own styles, so it works in projects with or without Tailwind.

**Can I use affectUI with v0, Cursor or Claude?** Yes. affectUI has an MCP server and llms.txt, so coding assistants can search the library, read the docs and add components for you.

---

## Comparison: affectUI vs AI Elements

AI Elements is Vercel's set of chat and agent building blocks, built on shadcn/ui and Tailwind CSS and made for the AI SDK. affectUI is a set of finished, designed components for AI products – including agent views AI Elements doesn't have, like agent trees, trace waterfalls, approval inboxes and cost ledgers – each one .tsx file without Tailwind or other dependencies. Use AI Elements for chat tied closely to the AI SDK, affectUI for the product around it, or either one alone.

### What each one is



- AI Elements – Vercel's component registry for AI apps: conversation, message, prompt input, reasoning, tool, sources and citations, plus pieces for code, voice and workflow canvases. Built on shadcn/ui, styled with Tailwind CSS 4, made to work with the AI SDK
- affectUI – 126 components, screens, blocks, illustrations and motion effects for AI products, each a single .tsx file with its own CSS and motion. UI only with plain props, so it works with any backend

### Where they differ



- Setup: AI Elements expects React 19, Tailwind CSS 4, an initialized shadcn/ui and the AI SDK; affectUI needs React 19 and nothing else
- Backend: AI Elements is shaped around the AI SDK's messages and status; affectUI components take plain props, so the AI SDK, LangGraph or your own API fit the same way
- Look: AI Elements takes on your shadcn/ui theme and stays plain; affectUI ships designed states and motion, in two styles (classic and clean)
- Scope: AI Elements covers chat, code and workflow canvases; affectUI goes further into multi-agent work – agent trees, lanes, handoffs, queues, findings, cost and token ledgers, approvals, autonomy settings – and adds full app screens
- Price: AI Elements is free; affectUI has 40 free MIT items and a one-time Pro license for the rest

### AI Elements is moving into shadcn/ui

As of October 2026, the AI Elements site says the project is moving to shadcn/ui and will be deprecated at the end of November 2026, and points new projects to install it from shadcn/ui. If you start a project now, check there for where the components live. affectUI isn't affected: it installs through the shadcn CLI from its own registry either way.

### Using affectUI with the AI SDK

affectUI components don't read AI SDK state themselves – you pass it in as props. A tool part from useChat, for example, maps straight onto the Tool Call Card:

```
import { ToolCallCard } from "@/components/ui/tool-call-card";

// inside message.parts.map(...)
if (part.type.startsWith("tool-")) {
  return (
    <ToolCallCard
      key={part.toolCallId}
      name={part.type.slice(5)}
      status={part.state === "output-available" ? "success" : part.state === "output-error" ? "error" : "running"}
      args={part.input}
      result={part.output}
      error={part.errorText}
    />
  );
}
```

### Which to pick



- You want chat that follows your shadcn/ui theme and is wired to the AI SDK with little code – AI Elements
- You want the product to look finished, or you need agent views beyond the chat – traces, agent trees, approvals, costs – affectUI
- You don't use Tailwind or the AI SDK – affectUI, since it needs neither
- Both work in one project: they install through the same shadcn CLI into different folders

affectUI: [Agent Tree](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-tree), [Trace Waterfall](https://www.affectui.com/components/trace-waterfall), [Tool Call Card](https://www.affectui.com/components/tool-call-card)

### Questions

**Is affectUI built on AI Elements?** No. affectUI components are self-contained and don't import AI Elements, shadcn/ui or Tailwind. Both install through the shadcn CLI, so they can live in the same project.

**Does affectUI work with the Vercel AI SDK?** Yes. The components take plain props such as status, text, arguments and results, so you map what useChat or streamText returns onto them – see the tool call example above.

**Does affectUI need Tailwind CSS?** No. Each component carries its own CSS with color variables, so it works with or without Tailwind.

**Which is free?** AI Elements is free. affectUI has 40 free, MIT-licensed items – among them Tool Call Card, Thinking Loader and Message Actions – and a one-time Pro license for the rest.

---

## Comparison: affectUI vs assistant-ui

assistant-ui is a chat framework: primitives such as Thread, Composer and Message plus runtimes that connect them to the AI SDK, LangGraph and other backends, MIT-licensed, with an optional Assistant Cloud for thread history. affectUI is not a runtime – it is finished, designed components for AI products, especially for agent work beyond the chat thread. Pick assistant-ui when you want chat state handled for you, affectUI when you want the views to look finished – or use both.

### What each one is



- assistant-ui – a React library for AI chat: composable primitives, runtimes for the AI SDK, LangGraph and custom backends, streaming, auto-scroll, retries, attachments and tool UIs. MIT, with an optional hosted Assistant Cloud
- affectUI – 126 components, screens, blocks, illustrations and motion effects for AI products, each a single .tsx file with its own CSS and motion, taking plain props

### Where they differ



- Kind: assistant-ui keeps the chat state – messages, branches, streaming – and renders it; affectUI renders what you pass in and leaves state to you
- Install: assistant-ui adds its npm packages, a runtime adapter, shadcn/ui components and Tailwind-based styles; affectUI adds one .tsx file per component and needs only React 19
- Scope: assistant-ui centers on the chat thread and the tool UIs inside it; affectUI covers the chat parts and the rest of an agent product – agent trees, traces, approvals, inboxes, costs and app screens
- Look: assistant-ui gives shadcn-style defaults you restyle; affectUI ships designed states and motion in two styles
- Price: assistant-ui is MIT with an optional paid cloud; affectUI has 40 free MIT items and a one-time Pro license

### Using both together

assistant-ui lets you render a tool call with your own component, and that is a good place for affectUI: show a running tool as a Tool Call Card, or a call that needs a person as an Approval Card. Outside the thread, affectUI's agent views – a trace, an agent tree, a decision inbox – sit next to it in the same app.

affectUI: [Tool Call Card](https://www.affectui.com/components/tool-call-card), [Approval Card](https://www.affectui.com/components/approval-card), [Decision Inbox](https://www.affectui.com/components/decision-inbox)

### Which to pick



- You want a working chat with branching, retries and persistence quickly, and will style it yourself – assistant-ui
- You already have the chat state (from the AI SDK, LangGraph or your API) and want UI that looks finished – affectUI
- Your product is more agent than chat – runs, traces, approvals, several agents – affectUI covers those views

affectUI: [Agent Inbox](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-inbox), [Trace Waterfall](https://www.affectui.com/components/trace-waterfall), [Chat Composer](https://www.affectui.com/components/chat-composer)

### Questions

**Is affectUI an alternative to assistant-ui?** Partly. Both have chat UI, but assistant-ui is a framework that manages chat state, while affectUI is components that render your state. They fit together: assistant-ui for the thread, affectUI for tool calls, approvals and agent views.

**Does affectUI have a runtime or backend?** No. affectUI is UI only. Connect it to the AI SDK, LangGraph, assistant-ui or your own API by passing props.

**Does affectUI need Tailwind or shadcn/ui?** No. It installs through the shadcn CLI, but each component carries its own CSS and doesn't import shadcn/ui.

---

## Comparison: affectUI vs CopilotKit

CopilotKit is a framework that connects an agent backend to your app: a chat, shared state between agent and UI, generative UI and human-in-the-loop, over its AG-UI protocol and for many agent frameworks. It is MIT-licensed, with paid hosted and Intelligence plans. affectUI is not a framework – it is finished, designed components for AI products that render the data you pass in. Use CopilotKit for the connection to the agent, affectUI for how the agent's work looks, or both together.

### What each one is



- CopilotKit – an SDK between your agents and your users: a customizable chat, tool calls that render UI, generative UI, shared state and human-in-the-loop, for React, Angular, Vue, mobile, Slack and Teams. It connects to agent frameworks such as LangChain, Mastra, CrewAI, Google ADK and the Claude and OpenAI agent SDKs through AG-UI, the protocol it created. MIT, with paid hosted plans and CopilotKit Intelligence for persistent threads, memories and analytics
- affectUI – 126 components, screens, blocks, illustrations and motion effects for AI products, each a single .tsx file with its own CSS and motion. UI only with plain props, so it works with any backend

### Where they differ



- Kind: CopilotKit runs the loop between agent and app – messages, state, tool calls, pauses for approval; affectUI renders what you pass in and leaves the loop to you
- Install: CopilotKit adds its npm packages and needs an agent backend or its hosted cloud; affectUI adds one .tsx file per component and needs only React 19
- Scope: CopilotKit centers on the conversation and the UI an agent generates inside it; affectUI covers the chat parts and the views around it – agent trees, traces, lanes, inboxes, approvals, costs and app screens
- Look: CopilotKit's chat is meant to be restyled or replaced through slots and headless hooks; affectUI ships designed states and motion in two styles
- Price: CopilotKit's framework is MIT with paid hosted and Intelligence plans; affectUI has 40 free MIT items and a one-time Pro license

### Using both together

CopilotKit lets an agent's tool calls and requests for approval render your own components – that is where affectUI fits. Show a running tool as a Tool Call Card, a pause for approval as an Approval Card, and a plan the agent shares as Agent Plan. Outside the chat, affectUI's agent views read the same run data: a trace of the run, a tree of sub-agents, an inbox of background work.

affectUI: [Tool Call Card](https://www.affectui.com/components/tool-call-card), [Approval Card](https://www.affectui.com/components/approval-card), [Agent Plan](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-plan)

### Which to pick



- You need to wire an agent framework into your app, with shared state and generative UI – CopilotKit
- You already have the agent connection (AI SDK, LangGraph, your own API) and want the UI to look finished – affectUI
- Your product shows agents working in the background – runs, traces, several agents, approvals in an inbox – affectUI covers those views
- Both together: CopilotKit for the agent loop, affectUI for the components it renders

affectUI: [Agent Tree](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-tree), [Trace Waterfall](https://www.affectui.com/components/trace-waterfall), [Agent Inbox](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-inbox)

### Questions

**Is affectUI an alternative to CopilotKit?** Not really. CopilotKit connects agents to your app and manages the state between them; affectUI is the UI layer. They work together – CopilotKit can render affectUI components for tool calls and approvals.

**Does affectUI support AG-UI?** affectUI has no protocol of its own – it takes plain props. Map AG-UI events such as tool calls, steps and state updates to the components' props, the same way as with any other backend.

**Does affectUI need Tailwind or a runtime?** No. Each component carries its own CSS and needs only React 19. There is no runtime or backend to set up.

---

## Comparison: affectUI vs prompt-kit

prompt-kit is a free, MIT-licensed set of building blocks for AI chat – prompt input, message, markdown, reasoning, tool, steps, chain of thought and more – installed with the shadcn CLI on top of shadcn/ui and Tailwind CSS. affectUI covers the chat too, but goes further into agent work – agent trees, traces, approvals, inboxes, costs – and ships each component as one designed file without Tailwind or other dependencies. For a plain chat in your shadcn/ui theme, prompt-kit is enough; for agent views and a finished look, affectUI.

### What each one is



- prompt-kit – about 20 components for AI chat interfaces (prompt input, message, markdown, code block, chat container, reasoning, tool, steps, chain of thought, sources, file upload, feedback bar, loaders) and blocks such as a chatbot and tool calling. Built on shadcn/ui and Tailwind CSS, installed with the shadcn CLI, MIT
- affectUI – 126 components, screens, blocks, illustrations and motion effects for AI products, each a single .tsx file with its own CSS and motion

### Where they differ



- Setup: prompt-kit needs shadcn/ui set up first and Tailwind CSS, and some pieces pull in shadcn components and lucide-react; affectUI needs React 19 and nothing else
- Scope: prompt-kit focuses on the chat window; affectUI covers the chat and the agent product around it – multi-agent trees and lanes, trace waterfalls, approvals and autonomy, inboxes, cost and context views, app screens
- Look: prompt-kit takes on your shadcn/ui theme and stays plain so you style it; affectUI ships designed states and motion, in two styles (classic and clean)
- Price: prompt-kit is free; affectUI has 40 free MIT items and a one-time Pro license for the rest

### Where they overlap

Both have the basic chat pieces: a tool call, a reasoning or thinking state, a loader and actions under a message. If those are all you need and your app already runs on shadcn/ui and Tailwind, prompt-kit fits in with no extra styles. affectUI's free versions of these – Tool Call Card, Thinking Loader and Message Actions – work in any React project and come with their states and motion designed.

affectUI: [Tool Call Card](https://www.affectui.com/components/tool-call-card), [Thinking Loader](https://www.affectui.com/components/thinking-loader), [Message Actions](https://www.affectui.com/components/message-actions)

### Which to pick



- A chat in your shadcn/ui theme, styled yourself, free – prompt-kit
- Agent views beyond the chat – traces, agent trees, approvals, costs – affectUI
- A project without Tailwind, or one that should look finished without design work – affectUI
- Both in one project: they install through the same shadcn CLI, and affectUI's styles stay inside its own components

affectUI: [Agent Tree](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-tree), [Trace Waterfall](https://www.affectui.com/components/trace-waterfall), [Approval Card](https://www.affectui.com/components/approval-card)

### Questions

**Is affectUI an alternative to prompt-kit?** For the chat parts, yes – both have tool calls, thinking states and message actions. affectUI also covers agent views prompt-kit doesn't, such as agent trees, traces and approvals.

**Does affectUI need shadcn/ui or Tailwind CSS?** No. It installs through the shadcn CLI, but each component carries its own CSS and doesn't import shadcn/ui.

**Do both work with the Vercel AI SDK?** Yes. Both are UI components you feed with data – messages, status, tool arguments and results – from the AI SDK or any other backend.

---

## Comparison: affectUI vs Aceternity UI and Magic UI

Aceternity UI and Magic UI are mostly for landing pages – animated heroes, backgrounds, text effects and marketing sections, built with Tailwind CSS and Framer Motion. affectUI is mostly for the product itself – chat, agents, approvals, dashboards – plus a smaller set of landing illustrations and motion effects that need no animation library. For the marketing site, start with them; for the AI app behind the sign-in, affectUI fits better.

### What each one is



- Aceternity UI – animated components, blocks and templates for landing pages and marketing sites, built with Tailwind CSS and Framer Motion; many free components and a paid all-access plan
- Magic UI – open-source (MIT) animated components for landing pages – text animations, backgrounds, special effects – built with Tailwind CSS and Framer Motion, with a paid Pro tier of templates and premium components
- affectUI – 126 components, screens, blocks, illustrations and motion effects for AI products, each a single .tsx file with its own CSS and motion

### Where they differ



- Focus: Aceternity UI and Magic UI make a marketing page stand out; affectUI makes the product work – composer, tool calls, traces, approvals, tables, settings
- Dependencies: both build on Tailwind CSS and Framer Motion; affectUI components carry their own CSS and animate with CSS and the Web Animations API, without a motion library
- Motion: their effects are meant to be noticed; affectUI's motion is quiet and tells people what changed – a status that settles, a number that rolls, a row that slides in
- Price: all three have free components and a one-time paid tier

### Where they overlap

affectUI also has animated illustrations for feature cards and empty states, and motion effects such as Number Ticker, Text Reveal and Grid Background. They follow light and dark mode and need no Lottie files or animation library – useful when the landing page should look like the product.

affectUI: [Integration Beam](https://www.affectui.com/illustrations/integration-beam), [Model Wheel](https://www.affectui.com/illustrations/model-wheel), [Number Ticker](https://www.affectui.com/motion/number-ticker)

### Which to pick



- A landing page with a big animated hero – Aceternity UI or Magic UI
- The AI product itself – chat, agents, approvals, dashboards – affectUI
- Many teams use one of them for the marketing site and affectUI inside the app; they don't clash, since affectUI's styles stay inside its components

affectUI: [Chat Composer](https://www.affectui.com/components/chat-composer), [Agent Tree](https://www.affectui.com/components/agent-tree), [Approval Card](https://www.affectui.com/components/approval-card)

### Questions

**Is affectUI an alternative to Aceternity UI or Magic UI?** Only in part. affectUI has some landing illustrations and motion effects, but most of it is product UI for AI apps, which Aceternity UI and Magic UI don't focus on.

**Does affectUI need Framer Motion or Tailwind CSS?** No. Each component animates with CSS and the Web Animations API and carries its own styles, so it needs only React 19.

**Can I use affectUI with Magic UI or Aceternity UI in one project?** Yes. They install through the same shadcn CLI, and affectUI's CSS is scoped to its own class names.
